content: The British thermal unit (BTU or Btu) is a unit of energy commonly used in industries such as power generation, steam production, heating, and air conditioning. While it is still informally used in some metric English-speaking countries like Canada, the United Kingdom, and occasionally New Zealand, it is increasingly considered outdated. In scientific contexts and most other regions, the BTU has been replaced by the SI unit of energy, the joule (J). In North America, the term BTU is often used to describe the heat value or energy content of fuels, as well as the power output of heating and cooling systems, including furnaces, stoves, barbecue grills, and air conditioners. When used as a unit of power, it is typically expressed as BTU per hour (BTU/h), though it is often abbreviated simply as BTU, which can lead to confusion. In the United Kingdom and other parts of the world, the abbreviation BTU is also used. Historically, the unit MBTU was defined as one thousand BTUs, based on the Roman numeral M for 1,000. However, this can be confused with the SI prefix mega (M), which represents one million (1,000,000). To avoid this confusion, many engineers and companies use MMBTU to denote one million BTUs. Alternatively, other units such as the therm (representing 100,000 BTUs) and the quad (representing 10^15 BTUs) are also used. A BTU is defined as the amount of heat required to raise the temperature of one pound of liquid water by one degree Fahrenheit. For reference, one BTU is approximately equal to 1,055 joules. Additionally, one standard cubic foot of natural gas yields approximately 1,030 BTUs when burned, though this value can range between 1,010 and 1,070 BTUs depending on the quality of the gas. The BTU per hour (BTU/h) is the most commonly associated unit of power with the BTU. For example: 1 BTU/h is approximately equal to 0.293 watts. 1 horsepower is approximately equal to 2,544 BTU/h. 1 ton of cooling, a common unit in North American refrigeration and air conditioning applications, is equal to 12,000 BTU/h or approximately 3.51 kilowatts. In the United States, the BTU is often defined at 59°F (BTU59°F), while in the European Union, the BTUIT (International Table BTU) is used. For larger energy quantities, 1 kilowatt-hour (kWh) is approximately equal to 3,412 BTUs.
